mat: SIBAL cotton/fiberglass fabric, cotton jersey, PMMA
cond: Cygnus cargo vehicle, 17-19 m3 free volume, 20 cm/s concurrent flow
finding: Real-size spacecraft fires on Saffire IV-VI reached 1.5 to 3.2 kW - small by Earth standards, but big for a 17-19 m3 cabin.
impl: Design fire-response and cleanup systems around a few-kW fire in a closed module.
quote: Practical scale fires ranging from 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in unmanned spacecraft with free air volumes of 17 to 19 cubic meters.

finding: Cabin temperature only rose near the fire itself; the real danger was the rise in carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide across the whole cabin.
impl: Fire response should prioritise gas monitoring, masks and atmosphere scrubbing, not just heat.
quote: the human hazard from a fire in a spacecraft is very similar to terrestrial fires where the heat from the fire is not the principal hazard and rather the smoke and gaseous products are a much greater concern.

finding: A single burning PMMA sample raised cabin-wide carbon monoxide by 308-320 ppm - above NASA's 24-hour limit (100 ppm) and close to the 1-hour limit (425 ppm).
impl: One small plastic fire can make a whole module's air unsafe within an hour.
quote: For carbon monoxide the levels were well above the 24-hour SMAC and quite close to the 1-hour level.

finding: Both PMMA fires pushed cabin CO2 above NASA's 1-hour limit of 3 mmHg.
impl: CO2 scrubbing capacity must cover fire events, not just crew breathing.
quote: As can be seen in Table 2, the allowable CO2 level was exceeded by both of the PMMA tests on Saffire VI.

cond: far-field ionization smoke detector, 1 mg/m3 alarm threshold
finding: A detector away from the fire only reached a typical alarm level after 981 s (~16 min) - by then most of the toxic gas had already been released.
impl: Smoke alarms alone are too slow; add CO/CO2 sensing and place detectors near likely fire sources.
quote: a typical alarm threshold was only achieved at 981 seconds. By this time most of the hazardous gas release had occurred.

value: PMMA kept growing; fabric reached steady size
finding: Thin fabric flames quickly reached a steady size, but thick acrylic flames kept growing until the airflow was turned down.
impl: Thick plastics are the bigger long-duration threat; cutting ventilation is an effective response.
quote: The SIBAL sample (left image) achieved a steady size and spread rate quite rapidly where the two PMMA samples grew continuously until the flow speed was reduced.

finding: Nomex fabric did not ignite even in Saffire VI's oxygen-enriched, low-pressure atmosphere.
impl: Nomex remains a good choice for crew-cabin fabrics in exploration atmospheres.
quote: The Nomex sample did not ignite and so it will not be included in this paper.

cond: airflow cut off (quiescent) for 70 s, oxygen-enriched (~26% O2, ~71 kPa)
finding: Turning the airflow off did not quickly put out a burning cotton fabric in oxygen-enriched air.
impl: Shutting off ventilation is not a guaranteed extinguisher in exploration atmospheres; crews still need an active suppressant.
quote: Extinguishment of thin charring fuels at increased oxygen cannot be assumed to occur rapidly in quiescent conditions.

cond: 65 s reduced flow then 15 s no flow
value: yes; one flame re-ignited after 6.4 s
finding: A melting-plastic flame shrank when airflow was cut but survived 15 s of no flow, and in one case went out and re-ignited 6.4 s later.
impl: After a fire appears out, keep monitoring - melting plastics can re-ignite.
quote: Flame shrank during the reduced flow interval of 65 seconds but survived the 15 second no-flow interval.

finding: Reducing airflow to a small value (about 5 cm/s) rather than shutting it off completely can help disperse fuel vapour and cool the material so the fire goes out.
impl: Fire-response procedures could use a 'low-fan' mode instead of 'fans off'.
quote: In some circumstances, reducing air flow to a small value rather than quiescent conditions may be useful to disperse fuel vapor and help cool the material to enable extinction

finding: A flame jumped a 4.5 cm gap to ignite a nearby, already-warmed acrylic surface.
impl: Gaps between materials are not reliable firebreaks in microgravity; spacing rules need margin.
quote: In one case, a flame was seen to jump a 4.5 cm gap to ignite a previously warmed PMMA surface.

finding: Flames grew to a nearly steady length; downstream flames were then starved or extinguished by the 'oxygen shadow' of the upstream flame.
impl: Microgravity fires tend to stabilise in size rather than grow without limit, which helps size response equipment.
quote: Once a flame achieved its limiting size, downstream flames were inhibited or extinguished by the oxygen “shadow” of the upstream flame.

finding: Flames on thick plastic in orbit settled at a finite size instead of growing as in NASA's standard upward-burning ground test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1).
impl: Ground material-screening tests remain valid but must be interpreted carefully for spaceflight.
quote: Thick fuel flame growth was found to be dissimilar from that seen in NASA STD 6001 Test 1: concurrent flames established a finite size and did not grow further.

mat: SIBAL cotton/fiberglass and cotton fabric, 40 x 50 cm
cond: from normal air (23% O2, 98 kPa) to exploration-like air (31% O2, 54 kPa)
finding: Large fabric samples spread fire at 3.4-4.05 mm/s; moving to the oxygen-rich, low-pressure exploration atmosphere raised the rate only modestly (3.6 to 4.05 mm/s).
impl: Exploration atmospheres increase fabric fire spread, but not dramatically - useful baseline for Moon/Mars habitat design.
quote: Flame spread rate (mm/s) NA NA NA NA 3.6 3.4 4.05

finding: Acrylic fires grew steadily (0.22-0.38 mm/s), not explosively - growth stayed linear even in high oxygen, unlike the accelerating growth seen on Earth.
impl: Crews have more predictable response time than Earth fire models suggest.
quote: This linear growth rate is an important finding as it suggests that even in high oxygen conditions, low-gravity flame spread and growth will not be acceleratory.

finding: Across seven large fires, cabin pressure rose at most 1.31 mbar and average temperature at most 0.5 C.
impl: Heat and over-pressure are minor hazards in a module this size; toxic products dominate.
quote: Overall, the pressure rise and temperature change were small but the smoke particulate rose to substantial levels and the gaseous products also achieved hazardous levels.

cond: remote smoke sensor, 2 mg/m3 alarm threshold
finding: A distant smoke detector alarmed within 1.5-3.5 minutes for fabric fires, but took 17-27 minutes for acrylic fires.
impl: Slow-smoking plastic fires are the detection weak spot - they need closer detectors or gas sensors.
quote: Time to alarm (s) [aerosol = 2 mg/m3] 1083 1117 1037 1603 92 146 201

metric: CO already present when alarm sounded
finding: By the time the smoke alarm triggered, one acrylic fire had already raised cabin CO by 283 ppm and CO2 above its 1-hour limit.
impl: NASA concludes a lower alarm threshold or more smoke detectors would be needed for this spacecraft layout.
quote: These results suggest that implementing smoke detection in this spacecraft for these design fires would require either a lower threshold or additional smoke detectors to reduce the transport time.

cond: normal air (~21.5% O2), 20-25 cm/s concurrent flow
finding: The first-ever large spacecraft fire spread at a steady 1.8-2.3 mm/s, while the same fabric on Earth burned completely with accelerating spread.
impl: Microgravity fires spread steadily rather than accelerating, so response timelines can be planned.
quote: Flame spread over a large thin charring surface in low-gravity showed that steady flame spread was possible (unlike normal gravity).

cond: opposed flow (flame spreading into the wind), ~21% O2
finding: Spreading against the airflow, the fabric burned ~10 cm in orbit (0.98-1.3 mm/s) but essentially not at all in the matching ground test.
impl: For some flame directions, microgravity is MORE flammable than the ground test predicts - ground screening is not always conservative.

finding: Acrylic kept burning in orbit down to 13.5% oxygen, while on Earth it stopped at 15.4% - materials are flammable at lower oxygen in the weak airflow typical of spacecraft.
impl: Earth flammability tests are NOT conservative for slow-ventilation spacecraft zones; materials need derating.
quote: The minimum O2 concentration of 13.5 percent O2 at a of 8 to 12 s–1 is significantly lower than the observed upward flame spread limit of 15.4 percent O2

cond: opposed flow, low velocities unreachable on Earth
finding: Flames spread along acrylic rods in orbit at 17.5% oxygen, but not below 19% on Earth - and spread was appreciably faster in microgravity.
impl: Rods/cables in slow airflow are more flammable in space than ground tests indicate.
quote: While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.

cond: concurrent flow slowly reduced until the flame quenched
finding: Fabric flames only went out once the airflow was slowed to just 1-5 cm/s.
impl: Reducing ventilation can extinguish a fire, but only if airflow is cut almost completely.
quote: The quenching velocities are small (between 1 and 5 cm/s), and an accurate determination is necessary to resolve the slope of the quenching boundary.

metric: ignition delay vs standard test igniter time
finding: Near the flammability limit, materials took up to ~10 times longer to ignite than the igniter-on time used in NASA's standard ground test.
impl: Short-igniter ground tests may wrongly pass a material that would ignite with longer heating.
quote: The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.

finding: Blowoff limits measured on ISS matched short drop-tower tests very well, so cheap ground facilities can estimate space flammability limits.
impl: Drop-tower testing plus extrapolation is a practical way to screen new materials.
quote: Blowoff extinction limits from the ISS experiments agree well with Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop test limits.

finding: All three Nomex fire-barrier samples failed to ignite.
impl: Nomex is confirmed as a strong fire barrier for ISS and future vehicles.
quote: The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.

finding: A burning wax droplet was ejected from the melting candle - melting plastics can fling burning drops that may ignite other materials.
impl: Keep melting-type plastics away from other flammables; drips go in every direction in microgravity.
quote: If the melt viscosity is low enough, burning droplets can be ejected and possibly ignite other materials.

value: fuel rich (equivalence ratio ~1.3); CO/CO2 10x flue-gas levels
finding: Low-flow microgravity flames burn inefficiently and fuel-rich, producing about ten times more CO relative to CO2 than efficient combustion.
impl: Expect high CO from even small, slow microgravity fires; CO sensors are essential.
quote: The CO to CO2 ratios for these fires are an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases, indicating that these flames are not efficient.

cond: opposed flow at two O2 levels
value: independent of thickness; rises as O2 falls
finding: Below a critical airflow speed flames die from radiative heat loss; that speed doesn't depend on fuel thickness but rises as oxygen drops.
impl: A single airflow threshold per oxygen level can guide 'fans-down' fire response for many materials.
quote: Results from four different fuel thicknesses indicate that fuel thickness does not affect the critical velocity, which increases if the O2 level is decreased.

cond: O2 diluted with N2, CO2 or He, 0.7 and 1 atm
finding: Methanol droplet flames could not survive below about 12-13% oxygen, whichever inert gas was used.
impl: Lowering cabin oxygen to ~12% would extinguish alcohol fires - a candidate 'inerting' target for fire response.
quote: The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.

cond: 0.70-3.05 atm, O2 diluted with N2 and/or CO2
value: early tests had contaminated fuel needles
finding: In the early FLEX tests a needle coating contaminated the fuel; 'disruptive' extinction of methanol was probably caused by this, though extinction diameters were barely affected.
impl: Treat FLEX 'Disruption' outcomes (2009-2011) with caution when ranking suppressants.
quote: (4) Disruptive extinction of methanol is probably due to the presence of the contaminant.

mat: Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber, Pyrell
cond: overheated below ignition, 0-8 cm/s flow, smoke aged 11-1800 s
finding: Smoke from overheated spacecraft materials was mostly 200-400 nm particles - small enough for ionization detectors to see easily.
impl: Detectors tuned to larger (micron) particles may miss early-stage smoke.
quote: Overall the majority of the average smoke particle sizes were found to be in the 200 nm to 400 nm range with the quiescent cases producing some cases with substantially larger particles.

metric: particle size, no flow vs 8 cm/s
finding: With no airflow, smoke particles were 2-3 times larger than with normal 8 cm/s ventilation - something that can't happen on Earth because smoke rises.
impl: Smoke looks different depending on whether fans are running; detectors must handle a broad range of sizes.
quote: The zero flow conditions produced smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate.

finding: Because smoke size varies so much by material and age, NASA found detectors measuring more than one property of the particle-size distribution work better and give fewer false alarms.
impl: Next-generation spacecraft detectors should combine ionization-type and light-scattering-type sensing.
quote: These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejection than single moment detectors.

finding: For Teflon smoke the ISS light-scattering detector gave only a weak signal, while the Shuttle-style ionization detector responded strongly.
impl: The ISS detector design can under-respond to small-particle smoke from some materials.
quote: Note weak scattering (ISS) detector signal but ionization (STS) is still strong

finding: The ISS cabin air is very clean - background particle levels are well below the Space Shuttle and typical buildings on Earth.
impl: Low background means detector alarm thresholds can be set lower, giving earlier warning.
quote: The ISS cabin was found to be a very clean environment with particulate levels substantially below the space shuttle and typical ground-based environments.

finding: Earlier Shuttle tests showed smoke particles can be larger in low gravity and that ISS and Shuttle detectors perform differently there - yet all spacecraft detectors had been designed from Earth data.
impl: Detector designs need microgravity smoke data, not just ground data.
quote: Recent space shuttle experiments confirmed that, in some cases, increased particles sizes are seen in low-gravity and that the relative performance of the ISS (International Space Station) and space-shuttle smoke-detectors changes in low-gravity

cond: still air (no flow), elevated O2 and reduced pressure
finding: Flames mimicking burning plastics self-extinguished in still air below ~25% oxygen, but burned for minutes in the oxygen-enriched atmospheres planned for future spacecraft.
impl: Exploration atmospheres (26.5-34% O2) remove the 'fire puts itself out in still air' safety margin that ISS air provides.
quote: While the flames can burn for minutes in elevated oxygen concentrations, like those being considered for future spacecraft, they were found to self-extinguish in concentrations below ~25% (by volume).

finding: Even at high oxygen, larger flames generally went out on their own within 1.5 minutes, and methane flames within a minute; small ethylene flames could burn for minutes.
impl: Small, low-heat-loss fires are the persistent ones - they can smoulder unnoticed in still air.
quote: While smaller flames can burn for minutes at elevated oxygen concentrations, larger flames were generally seen to self-extinguish within 1.5 minutes.

finding: Sooty microgravity flames contained several times more soot than matching Earth flames, and were taller and wider; dilute flames were also more stable, burning at lower fuel concentrations.
impl: Microgravity fires can be smokier and harder to blow out than Earth experience suggests.
quote: For sooty attached flames, preliminary results have revealed that the soot volume fraction can be several times greater in microgravity flames than in comparison normal-gravity flames.

value: grows then oscillates and radiatively extinguishes
finding: Large flames kept growing until radiative heat loss put them out, passing through an unstable phase where they partially quenched and reformed.
impl: A flickering/oscillating flame may be close to going out - useful cue for automated fire monitoring.
quote: large flames increase in size over time until the flame extinguishes because of radiative heat loss.

finding: Non-premixed cool flames - discovered in ISS droplet tests in 2012 - were also seen with n-butane gas, appearing after the hot flame went out.
impl: An apparently extinguished fire can keep reacting as an almost invisible cool flame.
quote: Cool flames were discovered in CFI-G testing with n-butane as can be seen in Fig. 10 which features a sequence of images from an intensified camera filtered for formaldehyde emissions.

value: weak fields stabilise dilute flames; soot can be suppressed
finding: Very weak electric fields could stabilise highly diluted flames, and soot generation could be suppressed.
impl: Spacecraft electrical fields could unexpectedly keep marginal flames alive - or be used to control them.
quote: It was found that highly diluted flames can be stabilized with very weak electric fields.

cond: 1-g at 40-100 kPa vs microgravity at 100 kPa, 20 cm/s flow
metric: low-pressure ground test as microgravity stand-in
finding: Lowering the air pressure in Earth tests weakens buoyancy and slows flame spread toward what is seen in microgravity - a cheap way to approximate space (and partial-gravity) fire behaviour.
impl: Low-pressure ground chambers can help screen materials for Moon/Mars gravity, with care because chemistry changes at very low pressure.
quote: Results show that reductions of pressure slow down the flame spread over the PMMA surface approaching that in microgravity.

finding: Earth's buoyancy adds the equivalent of a ~17 cm/s airflow to every flame; correcting ground blowoff limits for it lines them up with ISS results.
impl: NASA proposes a new 'upward flame spread test' that extrapolates ground data to predict microgravity flammability limits.
quote: which for the base rod size corresponds to a forced flow velocity of 17 cm/s, in good agreement with buoyant flow velocity estimates.

value: silica ash layer insulates fresh fuel
finding: Burning silicone deposits a silica ash layer on unburned material that can stop the flame; when airflow carried the ash away, thin silicone burned its full length.
impl: Silicone's fire resistance depends on airflow direction - it is not inherently non-flammable.
quote: The reason for the increased flammability in the downward direction compared to upward is attributed to the deposition of a silica layer onto the fresh fuel in the upward case.

cond: Cygnus cabin, NIST FDS fire model
finding: A standard fire-simulation code (NIST FDS) reasonably predicted how CO2 spread through the spacecraft cabin after the fires.
impl: Validated models can be used to plan detector placement and fire response for new Moon/Mars vehicles.
quote: The model did a reasonable job of predicting the CO2 data, while over-predicting in some cases.

finding: The thick acrylic sample on Saffire IV did not go out when planned, forcing the remaining tests to be cancelled.
impl: Thick plastics can outlast planned 'starve it of airflow' tactics - plan a backup suppressant.
quote: The PMMA in event number 5 did not extinguish when planned, causing the cancelation of other events.

value: still air: less flammable; with airflow: much more
finding: In completely still air, thin materials are less flammable in microgravity than on Earth - but adding even a gentle ventilating flow greatly widens their flammability range and spread rate.
impl: Spacecraft ventilation is the key variable: fans that keep crews alive also keep fires alive.
quote: Experiments conducted in spacecraft and drop towers show that thin-sheet materials have reduced flammability ranges and flame-spread rates under quiescent low-gravity environments (microgravity) compared to normal gravity.

finding: Low-gravity flames may be put out more easily by diluting the atmosphere or reducing cabin pressure than Earth flames.
impl: Inert-gas flooding or partial venting are promising spacecraft fire responses.
quote: Furthermore, low-gravity flames may be suppressed more easily by atmospheric dilution or decreasing atmospheric

mat: oxygen jet from oxygen generator; ethane jet flames
value: large soot output, hard to extinguish
finding: The 1997 Mir fire - fed by a leaking oxygen generator - produced large amounts of soot and was difficult to extinguish; follow-up tests showed oxygen enrichment raises soot and flame brightness.
impl: Oxygen storage and generators are a top fire risk; oxygen-enriched fires are smokier and harder to fight.
quote: They produced large amounts of soot and were difficult to extinguish.

finding: NASA's fire modellers note that normal-gravity testing is not necessarily the worst case, and terrestrial detection standards don't necessarily apply in spacecraft.
impl: Moon/Mars vehicle safety cases need microgravity/partial-gravity evidence, not just Earth certification.
quote: Normal gravity testing not necessarily worst-case
